title: timeline-spine — dated entries alternating across one vertical centre line
idea: A vertical hairline runs down the middle of the band, and dated entries sit alternately to its left and right, each anchored to the spine by a small marker at its own height. The visitor reads a history — a founding story, a restoration log, a season by season record — as a single descending line rather than as a row or a grid.
why_new: It is not step-rail, whose connector runs horizontally across the band and carries an ordered process at one height; it is not list-with-thumbnails or index-table, which stack rows in one aligned column with a shared rhythm and no centre axis. The alternating left/right anchoring around a vertical axis is a shape none of those can draw, because each of them commits to one column edge.
built_from: An outer group for the band, a heading and a lead paragraph, then one columns block per entry (two columns: text on one side, empty spacer on the other, order flipped entry to entry), each holding a heading, a short paragraph and a date paragraph. One reviewed CSS hook, .wp-block-group.is-style-timeline-spine, paints the centre hairline as a pseudo-element on the group, draws the marker dot on each row, and at 390px collapses the spine to the left edge so every entry stacks in one ordered column.
risk: The band needs a real dated sequence. If the brief has no dates, the entries become undated paragraphs floating either side of a decorative line and the composition reads as arbitrary zig-zag. It also fails if entries are wildly uneven in length — one long block on one side leaves a tall empty gap opposite, and with fewer than three entries the spine looks like a stray rule.
